title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Compare how far apart the particles are in a gas and in a liquid. What fills most of a gas that a liquid does not have?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Temperature sets the average kinetic energy. If the particles slow down, how do their hits on the walls change? The rigid volume cannot change.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Same temperature means the same average kinetic energy. Compare the molar masses: lighter particles must move faster to carry the same energy.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Pressure comes from particles hitting the walls. (a) More particles means more hits. (b) Heating makes each particle faster: think about how hard and how often they hit.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Use 1 atm = 760 mmHg as a conversion factor, with atm on the bottom so it cancels. Keep three significant figures.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Go through atm: divide by 101.325 kPa per atm first, then multiply by 760 mmHg per atm.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Set up a conversion factor with 1 atm on top and 760 mmHg on the bottom so mmHg cancels.
why: Since 1 atm = 760 mmHg exactly, dividing by 760 converts mmHg to atm, and the answer keeps the three significant figures of 118 mmHg.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Temperature and moles stay constant, so P and V are inverse: P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. Predict first: a bigger volume means a lower pressure.
why: At constant temperature and moles, Boyle's law gives P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub>; the volume grew 2.5 times, so the pressure fell to 1/2.5 of its value.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: A rigid tank means V is constant: Gay-Lussac's law, P<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>. Convert both temperatures to kelvins first (add 273.15).
why: With volume and moles constant, pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature, so P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub> × T<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> with 318.15 K and 293.15 K, and warming raises the pressure.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Constant pressure: Charles's law, V<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>. Change both temperatures to kelvins; −196 °C has no decimal places, which limits the significant figures.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Cross out what stays the same from P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub>/(n<sub>1</sub>T<sub>1</sub>) = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>/(n<sub>2</sub>T<sub>2</sub>). The unknown n<sub>2</sub> lands in a denominator, so flip both sides.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Pick easy numbers, such as V<sub>1</sub> = 1 L, T<sub>1</sub> = 400 K, and T<sub>2</sub> = 200 K, and put them into V<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: One set of conditions, so use PV = nRT solved for V. Convert 30.0 °C to kelvins and use R = 0.082058 L·atm/(mol·K).
why: With one set of conditions, V = nRT/P, using T = 303.15 K; R = 0.082058 L·atm/(mol·K) with P in atm leaves the answer in liters.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Solve PV = nRT for n. Change 21.0 °C to kelvins, and put R × T in parentheses on the calculator.
why: n = PV/(RT) with T = 294.15 K; P in atm and V in liters match R = 0.082058 L·atm/(mol·K), so only moles are left.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Our goal is the mole: change grams to moles with the molar mass of CO<sub>2</sub>, then use 22.4 L/mol, which works because the gas is at STP.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: At STP, 22.4 L/mol gives the moles; grams divided by moles gives the molar mass. The gas is diatomic, so halve it before looking at the periodic table.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Look for subscripts. (a) One set of conditions: PV = nRT. (b) Two temperatures, so the gas changes: cross V and n out of the combined gas law. Use kelvins.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Our goal is the mole: grams of Mg to moles, mole ratio to H<sub>2</sub>, then V = nRT/P with T in kelvins. This is not STP, so not 22.4 L/mol.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Grams of CaCO<sub>3</sub> to moles, then the mole ratio to CO<sub>2</sub>. The gas is at STP, so 22.4 L/mol turns moles into liters.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Both gases are at the same temperature and pressure, so the coefficients are volume ratios. Read the ratio of O<sub>2</sub> to CO from the equation.
why: At the same T and P, equal volumes hold equal moles (Avogadro's law), so the 1 : 2 coefficient ratio of O<sub>2</sub> to CO is also a volume ratio, and liters go straight to liters.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Subtract water's vapor pressure from the total first, so P belongs to the dry H<sub>2</sub>. Then n = PV/RT (mL to L, °C to K), the mole ratio, and the molar mass.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Which substance does V = nRT/P describe here? The n must be moles of that gas, which you get only after the mole ratio from the balanced equation.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Dalton's law: the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures. Round to the decimal place of the least precise value.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Find the mole fraction of CO<sub>2</sub> (its moles over the total moles), then multiply by the total pressure.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: The room pressure is shared by the oxygen and the water vapor. Subtract the vapor pressure, then round to the ones place, set by the room pressure.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Count particles: the mole fraction of B is its particles over all the particles. Multiply that fraction by the total pressure.
why: Every particle contributes equally to the pressure, so B's share of the particles (3 of 12) is its share of the total: P<sub>B</sub> = X<sub>B</sub> × P<sub>total</sub>.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: At fixed V and T, the total pressure depends only on the total moles, not on which gas. Use P<sub>1</sub>/n<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>2</sub> with the new total moles.

title: Problem 10.1
hint: Compare each choice with the KMT list in Section 10.1. A gas spreads out to fill any container: what does that say about forces between its particles?

title: Problem 10.2
hint: Pressure is force per area. In KMT, what are gas particles constantly doing to the walls? Heating changes their speed, not their size.

title: Problem 10.3
hint: Answer with particles: how does temperature change how fast the air molecules move, and how hard and how often they hit the inside of the ball? Their number stays the same.

title: Problem 10.4
hint: Average kinetic energy is proportional to the Kelvin temperature. What must happen to the Kelvin temperature to double the kinetic energy? Do not switch to °C.

title: Problem 10.5
hint: (a) What sets the average kinetic energy? (b) With equal kinetic energy, lighter particles move faster: rank by molar mass. (c) Faster particles escape through small gaps sooner.

title: Problem 10.6
hint: An ideal gas has particles that take up no space and do not attract each other. Which pressure keeps particles far apart, and which temperature makes attractions unimportant?

title: Problem 10.7
hint: Use 1 atm = 760 mmHg with mmHg on the bottom. Check: at 4,000 ft there is less air above you, so should the answer be above or below 1 atm?

title: Problem 10.8
hint: (a) Divide by 14.7 psi per atm. (b) The gauge reads above the outside pressure, so add the 1.00 atm of air. (c) Use 101.325 kPa per atm.

title: Problem 10.9
hint: Convert every choice to the same unit (atm is easiest), then compare. A big number in a small unit can still be a smaller pressure.

title: Problem 10.10
hint: (a) How do torr and mmHg compare? (b) Go through the base unit: 760 mmHg = 1 atm = 101.325 kPa. Keep two significant figures, like the readings.

title: Problem 10.11
hint: Find the pressure from the water (depth × 1 atm per 10.1 m), then add the air pressing on the surface of the water.

title: Problem 10.12
hint: (a) Divide by 760 mmHg per atm, then use 101.325 kPa per atm. (b) Summit pressure ÷ sea-level pressure × 100%. (c) At the same T and V, the number of molecules is proportional to the pressure.

title: Problem 10.13
hint: (a) As P goes up, what does V do? (b) Try both P × V and V/P for each trial; which stays the same? (c) Use P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>.

title: Problem 10.14
hint: Constant temperature and moles: Boyle's law, P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. Predict first: as the pressure drops on the way up, what happens to the volume?

title: Problem 10.15
hint: Charles's law, V<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>, with both temperatures in kelvins (add 273.15). Then redo it with °C and look at the sign of the result.

title: Problem 10.16
hint: Rigid means constant volume: Gay-Lussac's law, P<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>. Convert both temperatures to kelvins; a 27 °C rise should raise the pressure only a little.

title: Problem 10.17
hint: Constant T and P: Avogadro's law, V<sub>1</sub>/n<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>2</sub>. The volume grows, so the moles must grow by the same factor.

title: Problem 10.18
hint: For each one, ask which two variables change and which stay constant (rigid means constant V; a flexible container stays near constant P). Then decide direct or inverse.

title: Problem 10.19
hint: Put both pressures in the same unit and both temperatures in kelvins. Predict: lower pressure and higher temperature both make the volume bigger.

title: Problem 10.20
hint: Use V<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>1</sub> × (P<sub>1</sub>/P<sub>2</sub>) × (T<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>1</sub>) with easy numbers: P<sub>1</sub> = 1, P<sub>2</sub> = 3, T<sub>1</sub> = 1, T<sub>2</sub> = 2.

title: Problem 10.21
hint: The can's volume is fixed: Gay-Lussac's law. Convert both temperatures to kelvins (650. °C is known to the ones place), then compare with what °C would predict.

title: Problem 10.22
hint: Pressure and temperature both change, so use the combined gas law, V<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>1</sub> × (P<sub>1</sub>/P<sub>2</sub>) × (T<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>1</sub>), with kelvins.

title: Problem 10.23
hint: One set of conditions: n = PV/RT. The gas is not at STP, so 22.4 L/mol does not apply, and T must be in kelvins.

title: Problem 10.24
hint: Our goal is the mole: change grams of CO<sub>2</sub> to moles first. Then V = nRT/P with T in kelvins.

title: Problem 10.25
hint: Find P = nRT/V with T in kelvins; with R = 0.082058 the pressure comes out in atm. Then convert atm to mmHg; there are more mmHg than atm.

title: Problem 10.26
hint: Grams of N<sub>2</sub> to moles first, then solve PV = nRT for T = PV/(nR). That gives kelvins; subtract 273.15 for °C.

title: Problem 10.27
hint: At STP, 1 mol of any gas fills 22.4 L. Set up moles × (22.4 L / 1 mol) so moles cancel; the molar mass is not needed.

title: Problem 10.28
hint: (a) 25.0 °C is not STP, so use V = nRT/P. (b) Percent error = (student's value − correct value) ÷ correct value × 100%. (c) Solve PV = nRT for T.

title: Problem 10.29
hint: Find n from PV = nRT (kelvins, atm, liters), then M = grams ÷ moles and match it to the list. Density is simply grams over liters.

title: Problem 10.30
hint: A gas whose molar mass is larger than air's (about 29 g/mol) is denser than air and sinks. Compare each molar mass with 29.

title: Problem 10.31
hint: Density is grams per liter, and at STP one mole fills 22.4 L. Multiply g/L by L/mol so liters cancel and g/mol remains.

title: Problem 10.32
hint: (a) Divide by 14.7 psi per atm. (b) n = PV/RT with T in kelvins; carry the unrounded pressure. (c) Same temperature before and after: Boyle's law, no R needed.

title: Problem 10.33
hint: Moles of butane, then the mole ratio of O<sub>2</sub> to butane from the coefficients, then 22.4 L/mol at STP. Burning a fuel takes more O<sub>2</sub> than fuel.

title: Problem 10.34
hint: Grams of glucose to moles, mole ratio to CO<sub>2</sub> (check the coefficients), then V = nRT/P. 30.0 °C and 0.975 atm are not STP.

title: Problem 10.35
hint: Same T and P, so the coefficients are volume ratios. Use the coefficients of the two substances in the question, O<sub>2</sub> and C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>.

title: Problem 10.36
hint: Not STP, so n = PV/RT gives the moles of CO<sub>2</sub>. Then use the mole ratios from the equation and each molar mass.

title: Problem 10.37
hint: Liters of O<sub>2</sub> at STP to moles (divide by 22.4 L/mol), the mole ratio 2 KClO<sub>3</sub> : 3 O<sub>2</sub>, then the molar mass of KClO<sub>3</sub>.

title: Problem 10.38
hint: Grams of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> to moles, the mole ratio to O<sub>2</sub> (check the coefficients), then V = nRT/P with T in kelvins.

title: Problem 10.39
hint: Grams to moles of NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, the 1 : 1 ratio to CO<sub>2</sub>, then V = nRT/P in kelvins (this is not STP). R gives liters; convert to mL.

title: Problem 10.40
hint: (a) Grams of CH<sub>4</sub> to moles, mole ratio to CO<sub>2</sub>, then V = nRT/P. (b) O<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> are at the same T and P, so use a volume ratio.

title: Problem 10.41
hint: Same T and P: the coefficients are a volume ratio. How many H<sub>2</sub> does each O<sub>2</sub> need? Go straight from liters to liters.

title: Problem 10.42
hint: Same T and P, so work in liters with the coefficients. (a) Find how much O<sub>2</sub> the NO needs and compare with what is there. Use the limiting gas for the rest.

title: Problem 10.43
hint: Divide the percent by 100 to get the mole fraction of N<sub>2</sub>O, then multiply by the total pressure. A partial pressure is always less than the total.

title: Problem 10.44
hint: (a) Dalton's law: add the partial pressures; round to the ones place. (b) Mole fraction = partial pressure ÷ total pressure. (c) What is added to inhaled air, and where does O<sub>2</sub> go?

title: Problem 10.45
hint: (a) Mole percents add up to 100. (b) Percent ÷ 100 = mole fraction; multiply by 760. mmHg. (c) Moles of CO = mole fraction × total moles.

title: Problem 10.46
hint: Subtract the vapor pressure of water at the temperature of the water (check which value that is) from the barometric pressure.

title: Problem 10.47
hint: For each trial: subtract the vapor pressure and convert to atm; moles of H<sub>2</sub> = moles of Mg (1 : 1); R = PV/(nT) in liters and kelvins. (c) Which number grows?

title: Problem 10.48
hint: To find the moles of one gas, use that gas's own partial pressure in PV = nRT, with T in kelvins.

title: Problem 10.49
hint: (a) Mole fraction × pressure. (b) Subtract the water vapor first, then take the O<sub>2</sub> fraction of what is left. (c) Repeat with the new fraction. (d) Charles's law, in kelvins.

title: Problem 10.50
hint: (a) Partial pressure of O<sub>2</sub> = mole fraction × P<sub>total</sub>. (b) Solve the same equation for P<sub>total</sub>. (c) Subtract the 1.00 atm of air first, then convert atm to meters with 10.1 m per atm.

title: Problem 10.51
hint: Each gas in a mixture acts as if it were alone. Did the moles of O<sub>2</sub>, the volume, or the temperature change?

title: Problem 10.52
hint: (a) Divide by 14.7 psi per atm. (b) Same temperature before and after: Boyle's law. (c) Volume ÷ flow rate. (d) n = PV/RT, then moles × molar mass.

title: Problem 10.53
hint: Our goal is the mole: grams of CO<sub>2</sub> to moles. Then P = nRT/V (convert atm to psi with 14.7 psi per atm) and V = nRT/P.

title: Problem 10.54
hint: (a) X × P<sub>total</sub>. (b) n = PV/RT using the O<sub>2</sub> partial pressure. (c) Mole ratio from the equation. (d) V = nRT/P; check with a volume ratio.

title: Problem 10.55
hint: (a) Subtract the water vapor, then convert to atm. (b) n = PV/RT; change mL to L. (c) 1 : 1 ratio, then molar mass. (d) Repeat with the full barometric pressure.

title: Problem 10.56
hint: (a) n = PV/RT, then M = grams ÷ moles. (b) Match the molar mass to the list. (c) Same T and P, so the coefficients are volume ratios.

title: Problem 10.57
hint: P and V are constant: cross them out of the combined gas law to get n<sub>1</sub>T<sub>1</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>T<sub>2</sub>. Use kelvins; warming pushes air out of an open jar.

title: Problem 10.58
hint: Charles's law with the unknown on the bottom: flip both sides, T<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>1</sub> = T<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>2</sub>. Convert 21.0 °C to kelvins first, and back to °C at the end.

title: Problem 10.59
hint: Look for subscripts. Is the gas changing, with before and after values, or is there just one set of conditions? Is there a mixture of gases?

title: Problem 10.60
hint: n = PV/RT (kelvins; parentheses around R × T), then M = grams ÷ moles. The element is diatomic, so halve the molar mass before checking the periodic table.

title: Problem 10.61
hint: Molar mass: 22.4 L/mol at STP gives moles; grams ÷ moles. Empirical formula: assume 100 g, change to moles, divide by the smaller. Then molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass.

title: Problem 10.62
hint: Subtract water's vapor pressure at 30.0 °C (Table 1 in Section 10.6). Then n = PV/RT for the H<sub>2</sub>, the mole ratio to Mg, and the molar mass.

title: Problem 10.63
hint: Count all the particles. Neon's share of the particles is its mole fraction; multiply it by the total pressure.

title: Problem 10.64
hint: Grams of He to moles. At fixed V and T, pressure is proportional to total moles: scale to the new total, subtract the helium, then convert moles of N<sub>2</sub> to grams.
